title: How to Have a More Sustainable Black Friday, According to Experts
author: Simmone Shah
body:
Black Friday is here—holding the promise of good deals and the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season.

But if you plan to shop the sales, take the time to think about what you really need—and what you plan to give. Americans spent $10 billion dollars on unwanted gifts in 2024. And last year, 65% of consumers reported returning a holiday gift, while 54% admitted to regifting an unwanted item. So, being more intentional about your holiday shopping can benefit both your wallet and the planet.

“We are in an era right now where things are very expensive, and so when we're talking about affordability and Black Friday, thinking about what's really going to serve us and make us happy is a great way of thinking about sustainability too,” says Shelie Miller co-director of the Center for Sustainable Systems at the University of Michigan. “Being thoughtful about what's happening to our bank accounts as well as the overall amount of stuff we're buying can be very helpful as far as guiding us to a better path forward.”

We spoke with experts about how best to avoid overconsumption and shop with sustainability in mind this Black Friday.

Plan your shopping—and stick to the list

Before you shop, create a list of what you’re looking for to avoid any unwanted impulse purchases. “Having a list and sticking to it can be helpful for curbing some of those impulsive consumptions when that impulsivity is sky high,” says Karen Winterich, professor of marketing at Penn State University.

When you’re shopping, think twice before jumping on any deals for items that weren’t on your list. “We often get sucked into buying because it feels like a good deal,” says Winterich. “It makes us feel good to get that deal, and then later we may actually feel regret. Like, ‘I got a good deal, but did I even need to buy in the first place?’”

To avoid feeling any regret, focus on how much you’re spending rather than how much you’re saving. “Even if we're saving a lot, we're still spending,” says Winterich. “If it's 90% off, but I don't need it, I'm not going to use it. Don't buy it.”

Be intentional with your gifts

If you’re buying gifts for the holiday season, take some time to think about the person you’re shopping for before you swipe your card.

“If you're buying for someone else, pause and think about the person and if [the gift] is something they would really want and enjoy and use, or if you’re buying it to check the box, and say, ‘I got them a gift,’” says Winterich.

If you know your friend has a cupboard full of coffee mugs, consider getting them locally roasted coffee beans or treating them to a coffee instead of buying them another mug.

Consider gifting something people can consume—especially if you’re buying for someone you don’t know very well, like an office Secret Santa or a new neighbor.

“Maybe that’s a loaf of local bread or something you make yourself with a locally made jam, or it could be some hot chocolate mix with a special treat attached to it,” says Winterich. “Something that's consumable and not necessarily made from plastics and shipped overseas, but a little bit more locally made, that they're going to consume and not have sitting around or donating. [It conveys] ‘I'm still thinking of you, I'm still giving you a gift, but it's not stuff that is going to sit there that you’re not going to enjoy and appreciate.”

Consider your footprint

Individual actions may not seem like much, but their impact can add up. Every year, people in the United States throw out more than 34 billion lbs of used textiles—roughly 100 lbs of textile waste per person each year—while global electronic waste continues to climb.

If you’re buying an item online, see if you can pick it up at the store. Last mile delivery, the final step before a product reaches your doorstop, is responsible for roughly half of a delivery’s total emissions. “If you know you're already going to be going to the store, maybe you could just pick out one day in the week and say I'm going to hit these couple stores up where I have items to pick up at, rather than having that individual last mile delivery,” says Winterich.

Consider shopping for quality rather than quantity—and be mindful of what you might already have at home. “A lot of times with impulse buys we're trying to get as much stuff for as little money as possible,” says Miller. “When we're talking about sustainability, we want people to use items for a long time to get their best environmental value.”

“Everything that we buy had [manufacturing and shipping] impacts that were many times bigger than the product itself,” continues Miller. “So [thinking] maybe that stocking stuffer isn't really going to bring joy, and it's just going to affect my pocketbook. That actually has some environmental [benefits] to it.”
